plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.2.9
plan.contextChunk: This figure is part of a worked example asking to evaluate the double integral of (2x - y^2) over the triangular region R enclosed between y = -x + 1, y = x + 1, and y = 3. The figure shows the triangular region R in the xy-plane with vertices at (-2, 3), (0, 1), and (2, 3); the bounding lines y = 3 (top), y = -x + 1 (lower left), and y = x + 1 (lower right) are labeled. The y-axis divides R into two sub-regions: R1 (shaded blue, left half) and R2 (shaded yellow, right half), each with a red vertical strip indicating the direction of inner integration. The figure illustrates the decomposition of R into two type-I sub-regions required when the lower boundary changes expression across the y-axis.

interactionPlan.concept: Decomposing a double integral into sub-regions (Type I) versus integrating over a single unified region by switching order (Type II).
elements: shaded region R1 (blue fill, left of y-axis)
shaded region R2 (yellow fill, right of y-axis)
vertical slicing indicators (red lines in R1 and R2)
horizontal slicing indicator (blue horizontal line for Type II)
labels R1, R2, and equations y = -x + 1, y = x + 1, y = 3

interactions.teaches: how choosing between Type I (vertical) and Type II (horizontal) slicing determines whether we must split the region of integration
interactions.label: Slicing Direction

interactions.teaches: how changing the lower boundary equations dynamically alters the region shape and shifts the corresponding integration limits
interactions.label: Lower Boundary Equations

demo_steps.title: Type I Splits the Region
demo_steps.narration: Integrating with vertical slices (Type I) requires splitting the triangle into sub-regions R1 and R2 at x = 0, because the lower boundary formula abruptly changes from y = -x + 1 to y = x + 1.

demo_steps.title: Explore Dynamic Boundaries
demo_steps.narration: Try editing the equations for the left and right boundaries. Observe how the shape of the regions and the corresponding integration limits automatically update.

demo_steps.title: Type II Simplifies Setup
demo_steps.narration: Switching to horizontal slices (Type II) allows a single continuous sweep from the left boundary x = y - 1 to the right boundary x = 1 - y, consolidating the problem into a single double integral.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Splitting integration regions is not always an inherent property of the shape itself, but rather a consequence of our slicing direction; switching integration order can often bypass piecewise decomposition entirely.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: An interactive coordinate system with origin (0,0). A triangular region is plotted with vertices at (-2,3), (0,1), and (2,3). In Type I mode, the y-axis splits the triangle: the left half (R1) is shaded light blue with a red vertical slice line, and the right half (R2) is shaded light orange with a red vertical slice line. In Type II mode, the entire triangle is shaded a uniform light green, with a horizontal blue slice running from the left boundary to the right boundary. Below or alongside the plot, render the corresponding double integral equations in real-time, showing the integration limits matching the chosen mode and input equations.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- equation_input for the two lower boundary equations: two fields pre-filled with "-x + 1" (left, for R1) and "x + 1" (right, for R2); when the learner edits either, the corresponding boundary line redraws, the shaded sub-regions R1 and R2 update, and the inner integral limits display — shows directly how the lower boundary formula changing expression at x=0 is what forces the decomposition into two sub-integrals
- toggle between Type I (vertical slices, R1 + R2 split with red strips) and Type II (horizontal slices, single region with blue horizontal strips and limits x from -(y-1) to (y-1)) — teaches that switching integration order eliminates the need to decompose R
